segments.text:
The file comment gives the design of the benchmark.
- Each thread allocates its own buffers and writes them first. The comment says that a timed interval therefore holds no page fault.
- All threads start an interval together at a barrier.
- Each thread runs whole passes over its buffer until the time of `--min-ms` has passed.
- GB means 1e9 bytes.
segments.heading: File header, includes, constants and data types

segments.text: `_GNU_SOURCE` makes Linux-specific calls visible, for example `sched_setaffinity`. Line 10 includes the header of the NEON intrinsics. This line is new against the old source [Ref2]. The source comment says that the file therefore builds on AArch64 only.

- `HUGE_BYTES`: 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes), the size of one huge page. Buffers are aligned to it.
- `MAX_CPUS`: the CPU list holds at most 1024 entries.
- `MAX_REPS`: at most 32 timed intervals per kernel.
- `CHECK_BYTES`: 8 MiB (8,388,608 bytes). It sets how many passes a thread runs between two clock reads (lines 452 to 454).

The six kernels. The numbers 0 to 5 fix the order in which one process runs the kernels that are selected. Each name is a value of `--kernel` and the first field of the rows that lines 601 and 605 print.

`cfg` holds the settings of the process. `bytes` is the buffer size of one thread. `run[k]` is 1 when kernel `k` is selected. The defaults in line 39 are 1 thread, a minimum interval of 0.5 s, 3 repetitions and a request for huge pages.
One `result` holds one timed interval of one thread: the bytes that the thread moved and its own elapsed time in seconds.
One `thread` record per benchmark thread: its index, its CPU, its buffers `a` and `b`, and one `result` per kernel and repetition. Only the copy kernels use `b`.
The barrier that all benchmark threads and `main` share. Line 559 sets its size to the number of threads plus 1.

Reads the Linux clock `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` and returns the time in seconds. This clock only moves forward. A change of the date does not change it. It is the only clock that the file reads: `worker` calls it in lines 471 and 476.
segments.heading: Function `now_s`: the clock

segments.text: Reads a number with an optional suffix `k`, `m` or `g`, in upper or lower case. The suffix multiplies by 2^10, 2^20 or 2^30. `256M` gives 268,435,456 bytes. A text without a number, other text after the suffix, or a value of 0 or below ends the program with exit status 2.
segments.heading: Function `parse_bytes`: the value of `--bytes`

segments.text: `strtok` splits the list at each comma. Each item is one number, a range `lo-hi`, or a range with a step `lo-hi:step`. `strtol` reads each number. When no digit follows `-` or `:`, lines 88 and 91 set `e` back to `tok`, and the test in line 94 then rejects the item.
segments.heading: Function `parse_cpus`: the value of `--cpus`

segments.text:
Rejects an item in each of these cases. The program then ends with exit status 2.
- The item holds no number, or other text follows the numbers.
- The start is negative, or the end is below the start.
- A CPU number is `CPU_SETSIZE` or above (the number of CPUs that the CPU set type of the C library can hold).
- The step is below 1.
Appends every CPU number of the item to `cfg.cpus` and counts it in `cfg.ncpus`. `--cpus 0-119` gives the 120 entries 0, 1, 2, ... 119. More than 1024 entries end the program with exit status 2.

Builds a CPU set that holds only `cpu` and passes it to `sched_setaffinity`. The first argument 0 means the calling thread. After the call Linux runs this thread on that CPU only. A failure ends the program with exit status 2.
segments.heading: Function `pin_cpu`: bind the calling thread to one CPU

segments.text:
- Line 121 rounds the size up to a multiple of 2 MiB.
- Lines 122 to 123 ask Linux for that size plus 2 MiB of new memory that no file backs (`mmap`). The extra 2 MiB leave room for the alignment in line 128.
- Linux assigns no physical page at this call. It assigns a page at the first access to it.
- A failed `mmap` ends the program with exit status 2.
segments.heading: Function `alloc_buf`: one buffer, aligned to 2 MiB

segments.text:
- Line 128 moves the start up to the next multiple of 2 MiB. The buffer then starts at the boundary of a huge page.
- Line 131 asks Linux to use huge pages for the buffer (`MADV_HUGEPAGE`). With `--no-thp` it forbids them (`MADV_NOHUGEPAGE`). Part A does not pass `--no-thp` [Ref5].
- A failed `madvise` only prints a message.
- The file never checks whether the buffer lies on huge pages.
- No code releases the buffer.

Line 136 opens a C comment that ends in line 166. The compiler reads nothing between these two lines. No preprocessor condition such as `#if` is used here. The comment keeps the three kernels of the old source as a record.
segments.heading: Old kernels, kept as text inside a comment (not compiled)

segments.text: Text of the old read kernel, the same text as in the old source [Ref2]. It is not compiled here. It adds each 8-byte word to one of 16 running sums and returns the total of the sums. The binary bw_old holds this code, and the binary bw_new does not [Ref1].
Text of the old `k_write` and the old `k_copy`: plain C loops over 8-byte words. They are not compiled here. Line 166 closes the comment.

- Each loop pass moves 256 B as 16 vectors of 16 B. It does no arithmetic on the data.
- The buffer size must be a multiple of 256 B and must not be 0. `main` checks this in line 549.
- The compiler chooses the machine code. The listing of the build on CRB shows the result [Ref1].
- Lines 175 to 182 explain the empty `asm` statement of `k_read` and `k_copy`. The rows of lines 205 and 261 repeat it.
segments.heading: Comment: design of the kernels that are compiled

segments.text:
- `a` is the start of the buffer. `n` is the number of 8-byte words in it.
- `noinline` forbids the compiler to merge the function into its caller. The listing therefore shows it as a function of its own [Ref1].
- The function returns nothing (`void`). The old `k_read` returned a sum.
- This is the only `k_read` that the compiler reads. The text in lines 143 to 153 is a comment.
segments.heading: Function `k_read`: the new read kernel

segments.text: `p` is the read position. `end` is the first address after the buffer: `a` plus `n` words. The machine code computes it with one instruction before the loop: `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3` [Ref1].
`do`: the loop body runs before the first test of the end. `main` rejects a buffer size of 0 (line 549), so the body never runs on an empty buffer.
Each `vld1q_u64(p + k)` loads 16 B, which is two 8-byte words, from word `k` after the read position into a vector variable. These 6 lines load the bytes 0 to 95 of the current block of 256 B.
The loads of the bytes 96 to 191 of the block.

- The loads of the bytes 192 to 255. One loop pass has 16 loads in the source. It reads 256 B, each byte once.
- gcc joined each two neighbour loads into one `ldp` instruction, which loads 32 B into two 16-byte registers.
- The machine loop has 8 `ldp` instructions at the byte offsets 0, 32, 64, ... 224, in rising order [Ref1].

- The instruction text of this `asm` statement is empty. It adds no instruction to the loop.
- It names the 16 vectors as inputs that must be in vector registers (`"w"`). So the compiler must have all 16 values loaded at this point.
- The source comment gives the purpose (lines 175 to 178): the statement keeps gcc from deleting the loads.
- After this line nothing uses the values. They are dropped. The listing shows no instruction that uses a loaded register, and no add of data [Ref1].
Moves the read position forward by 32 words, which is 256 B. Machine code: `add x0, x0, #0x100` [Ref1].

Repeats the loop while the read position is below the end. Machine code: `cmp x1, x0`, then `b.hi` back to the first `ldp`. One loop pass is 11 instructions for 256 B: 8 `ldp`, 1 `add`, 1 `cmp` and 1 branch [Ref1].
End of the function. No value is returned.

Stores the value `v` to every 8-byte word of the buffer. `vdupq_n_u64(v)` builds one 16-byte vector that holds `v` twice. In a process with the kernel `read` this function runs once per buffer, before any timing (line 459).
segments.heading: Function `k_write`: new write kernel, also the first write of a buffer

segments.text:
- Each loop pass stores the vector 16 times, which is 256 B. Then the position moves on by 256 B.
- gcc compiled the 16 stores to 8 `stp` instructions per loop pass. Each `stp` stores the 16-byte register q31 twice, which is 32 B [Ref1].
- The old `k_write` was a plain C loop. gcc compiled it to a loop of SVE instructions [Ref1].
Copies `n` words from `s` to `d`. `restrict` tells the compiler that the two buffers do not overlap. A process with the kernel `read` does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `k_copy`: the new copy kernel

segments.text: 16 loads of 16 B from the source buffer. The pattern is the same as in `k_read`.

The same empty `asm` statement as in `k_read`. The source comment (lines 178 to 182) says that the statement does not fix the order of the loads and the stores: gcc may move code across it. The comment reports what was observed with gcc 14.2.0: with the statement the 8 `ldp` loads of a loop pass come before the 8 `stp` stores, and without it loads and stores alternate. The listing of bw_new shows the 8 `ldp` before the 8 `stp` [Ref1].
16 stores of 16 B to the destination buffer. Then both positions move on by 256 B. The loop ends when the source position reaches the end of the source buffer.

- The whole loop of these three kernels is assembly text. The compiler copies it. It only puts a register in the place of each name such as `%[p]` [Ref1].
- One loop pass moves 256 B. `k_asmread` has 8 `ldp` and `k_asmwrite` has 8 `stp`, followed by `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`. `k_asmcopy` has 8 `ldp`, 8 `stp` and 2 `add`, followed by `cmp` and `b.lo`.
- The old source holds the same text for these kernels [Ref2]. Both binaries hold the same instructions for them [Ref1].
segments.heading: Hand-written kernels (`asm` text)

segments.text: `#if defined(__aarch64__)`: lines 295 to 376 are compiled only for AArch64. CRB is an AArch64 machine, so this branch is used and `HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` is 1. Proof: the listing of bw_new holds `k_asmread`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy` [Ref1].
`p` is the read position and `end` is the first address after the buffer, as in `k_read`.
segments.heading: Function `k_asmread`: the kernel `asmread`

segments.text:
- `1:` is the label at the start of the loop.
- 8 `ldp` instructions load 32 B each into the registers q0 to q15, at the byte offsets 0, 32, 64, ... 224. One loop pass reads 256 B.
- `add` moves the position on by 256 B.
- `cmp` and `b.lo 1b` branch back to the label while the position is below the end.
- Nothing uses the loaded values.

- `[p] "+r"(p)`: `p` is in a general register. The assembly text reads it and changes it.
- `[end] "r"(end)`: `end` is an input in a general register.
- The last list names what the text overwrites: the vector registers v0 to v15 and the condition flags (`cc`). The word `memory` in it tells the compiler that the text accesses memory that the other lists do not name.
- v8 to v15 are in that list. The Arm calling convention (AAPCS64) requires a function to keep their low halves d8 to d15 unchanged for its caller (source comment, lines 291 to 292). So gcc saves d8 to d15 before the loop and restores them after it, once per call [Ref1].
- The loop itself has 11 instructions per 256 B, as the loop of `k_read` has. The two loops differ in the register numbers and in the form of the compare and the branch [Ref1].
`dup` copies `v` into both halves of the register v0. Each loop pass stores 256 B with 8 `stp q0, q0` instructions. A process with the kernel `read` does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `k_asmwrite`: the kernel `asmwrite`

segments.text: Copies `n` words from `s` to `d` with a hand-written loop. A process with the kernel `read` does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `k_asmcopy`: the kernel `asmcopy`

segments.text: Each loop pass loads 256 B with 8 `ldp` instructions and then stores them with 8 `stp` instructions. Then both positions move on by 256 B.
The operand lists: both positions are read and changed, `end` is an input, and the text overwrites v0 to v15, memory and the condition flags.
The other branch of the `#if` in line 294. It would set `HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` to 0 on a machine that is not AArch64. The build on CRB does not use it.

Line 381 opens a second C comment that ends in line 415. It keeps the old `pass` as a record. It also says what the old `worker` had: a local variable `sink` that received the sum of the old `k_read`.
segments.heading: Old `pass`, kept as text inside a comment (not compiled)

segments.text: Text of the old `pass`. It is not compiled. Its fifth parameter `sink` pointed to a variable on the stack of the thread. Line 392 stored the sum of the old read kernel there, once per pass.
The rest of the old text. The `#if` in line 400 is inside the comment and has no effect. Line 415 closes the comment.

- Runs kernel `k` once over the whole buffer of thread `t`.
- Returns the number of bytes that this pass moved.
- `n` is the buffer size in 8-byte words. `v` is the value that the write kernels store.
- This is the only `pass` that the compiler reads. It has no `sink` parameter.
segments.heading: Function `pass`: one pass of one kernel over the buffer

segments.text: Kernel `read`: calls the new read kernel on buffer `a`. Then it returns `cfg.bytes`, the buffer size: 268,435,456 bytes (256 MiB) in the whole-chip test. The count is the size that the kernel was asked to read. Nothing is counted inside the kernel.
Kernel `write`: stores `v` to the whole buffer and counts the buffer size once.
Kernel `copy`: copies buffer `a` to buffer `b`. It counts 2 times the buffer size: the bytes read plus the bytes written.
`#if HAVE_ASM_KERNELS`: true on CRB, so lines 431 to 439 are compiled. Kernel `asmread`: calls the hand-written read loop and counts the buffer size.
Kernel `asmwrite`: counts the buffer size once.
Kernel `asmcopy`: counts 2 times the buffer size. `#endif` closes the condition of line 430.
Any other kernel number counts 0 bytes. On CRB all six kernels have a case, so this line is not reached.
The start function of every benchmark thread. `t` is the record of this thread. `main` filled its index and its CPU in lines 564 to 565.
segments.heading: Function `worker`: one benchmark thread

segments.text: `n` is the buffer size in 8-byte words. `--bytes 256M` gives 33,554,432 words.

`v` is the value that `k_write` stores. It depends on the process ID (`getpid`) and on the thread index. The source comment gives the reason: the compiler cannot replace the store loop by `memset`. The read kernels do not use `v`.

`passes_per_check` is the number of passes between two clock reads: 8 MiB divided by the buffer size, rounded down, and at least 1. With 256 MiB buffers the division gives 0, so the value is 1. A thread of the whole-chip test therefore reads the clock after every pass.
Binds this thread to its CPU when `--cpus` was given. In part A thread `i` is bound to CPU `i`, for `i` from 0 to 119 [Ref5].

- Maps buffer `a` and stores `v` to all of it with the new `k_write`.
- This first write makes Linux assign the physical pages of the buffer.
- It happens after the thread is bound to its CPU and before any timing.
- bw_old runs the old `k_write` at this place [Ref2].
A second buffer `b` is mapped and written only when a copy kernel is selected. A process with the kernel `read` has one buffer per thread.
Loop over the six kernels in the order of line 26. A kernel that is not selected is skipped. Every process of part A selects one kernel [Ref5].
One timed interval per repetition. Part A passes `--reps 3`, so every process times 3 intervals [Ref5].
Warm-up: one whole pass of the same kernel over the buffer. It is not timed. It runs before every interval, not only before the first one.
First barrier. The thread waits here until all benchmark threads and `main` (line 582) have arrived. Then the barrier lets all of them continue.
**Start of the timed interval.** The thread reads the clock into `t0` as its first step after the barrier. Every thread has its own `t0`.
`bytes` counts the bytes of this interval. `p` counts its passes.

Runs `passes_per_check` passes, which is 1 pass in the whole-chip test, and adds the byte count of each pass to `bytes`. The argument `v + p` changes the stored value from pass to pass. Only the write kernels use it.
Reads the clock into `t1` after the passes of lines 474 to 475. In the whole-chip test that is after every pass. The clock is never read inside a pass.

- **Stop rule.** The loop repeats until `cfg.min_s` or more has passed after `t0`. With `--min-ms 500` that is 0.5 s.
- The test comes only after a whole pass. So every thread ends its interval at the end of a pass, at its own time.
- The interval of a thread is 0.5 s or longer. It exceeds 0.5 s by less than the time between its last two clock reads, which is one pass here.
Stores the result of this thread for this interval: the bytes of its whole passes and its own elapsed time `t1 - t0`. The interval ended at the last clock read of line 476.

Second barrier. The thread waits here until all other threads have ended their interval and `main` (line 583) has arrived. A thread that waits here runs no kernel. The threads that are still in their last pass continue without it.
After the last interval of the last selected kernel the thread ends.
Prints the argument list to the error output and ends the program with exit status 2. The text of line 492 is new against the old source [Ref2]. It does not change a measurement.
segments.heading: Function `usage`

segments.text: The defaults before the arguments are read: a buffer of 1 MiB per thread and the three kernels `read`, `write` and `copy`.
segments.heading: Function `main`: arguments, threads, rates and output

segments.text: Loop over the arguments. `more` is true when one more argument follows. A flag with a value needs it.

- `--no-thp`: forbid huge pages for the buffers.
- `--per-thread`: print one more line per thread and interval.
- `--threads T`: the number of benchmark threads.
- `--cpus LIST`: the CPUs of the threads (`parse_cpus`).
- `--bytes B`: the buffer size per thread (`parse_bytes`).
- `--min-ms MS` and `--reps R`: the minimum length of a timed interval, stored in seconds, and the number of intervals per kernel.

`--kernel NAME` clears the selection and then selects one kernel. `all` and `asmall` select three kernels. An unknown name prints the usage text and ends the program. Every process of part A gets one of the six names `read`, `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite`, `asmcopy` [Ref5].
Any other argument prints the usage text and ends the program.
`--threads` is accepted only together with `--cpus`. When `--threads` is given without `--cpus`, the program prints a message and the usage text and ends with exit status 2.

The value checks: 1 thread or more, 1 to 32 repetitions, and a buffer size that is not 0 and is a multiple of 256 B. A value that fails prints the usage text and ends the program. The kernels need the size check: each loop pass moves 256 B.
Stops a process that selects an `asm` kernel on a machine without them. On CRB `HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` is 1, so this test never stops the program there.
Prints a warning, and continues, when there are more threads than CPUs in the list. Part A has 120 threads and 120 CPUs [Ref5].

Allocates the thread records, filled with 0. Creates the barrier for the number of threads plus 1: the benchmark threads and `main`. In part A that is 121. A failure of either step ends the program with exit status 2.

- Starts the benchmark threads. Thread `i` gets the index `i` and the CPU `cfg.cpus[i % cfg.ncpus]`. With `--threads 120 --cpus 0-119` that is CPU `i`.
- A thread that cannot be started ends the program with exit status 2.
- This file does not bind `main` to a CPU.

Prints the two header lines of the output: a comment line with the settings and the rate formula, and the line of column names. `thp=madvise` means that the program asked for huge pages. It does not show that the buffers got them.
Loop over the selected kernels, in the same order as in `worker`.
segments.heading: `main`: rate of each interval and the output rows

segments.text: `best` will hold the highest rate of the repetitions of this kernel. The inner loop runs once per timed interval.
First barrier wait of `main`. It ends when all benchmark threads have done their warm-up pass and have reached line 470. The barrier then lets all threads go into the timed interval.
Second barrier wait of `main`. It ends when every thread has ended its interval and has reached line 480. `main` waits here during the whole interval.
Start values for this interval: `total` (bytes of all threads), `max_el` (longest thread time), `mn` and `mx` (lowest and highest thread rate) and `sum` (sum of the thread rates).
Loop over the threads. `r` is the result that thread `i` stored in lines 478 to 479.
`g` is the rate of this one thread in GB/s: its bytes, divided by its own elapsed time, divided by 1e9.
Adds the bytes of the thread to `total`. Keeps the longest elapsed time of all threads in `max_el`.
Keeps the lowest and the highest thread rate. Adds the thread rate to `sum`.

- **The rate of the interval**, printed as `aggregate_GBps`: the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of any thread, divided by 1e9.
- A thread with a shorter elapsed time adds no bytes for the rest of that longest time.
- So this value is at most the sum of the thread rates. It is lower when the elapsed times of the threads differ.
Keeps the highest interval rate of this kernel in `best`.

One output row per interval, with 10 fields.
- 1 to 4: kernel name, number of threads, buffer size per thread in bytes, repetition number counted from 0.
- 5: `total_bytes`, the bytes of all threads.
- 6: `elapsed_s`, the longest thread time, with 4 decimals.
- 7: `aggregate_GBps`, with 2 decimals.
- 8 to 10: the lowest, the highest and the mean thread rate in GB/s, with 2 decimals.

After the last interval of the kernel: one row with `best` in field 4 and the highest interval rate in field 7. The fields 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 are empty. The statistics script of the rerun does not use this row [Ref7].
Only with `--per-thread`. Part A does not pass this flag, so its output holds no such lines [Ref5] [Ref6].

One line per thread and interval: the word `thread`, the thread index, its CPU, the kernel name, the repetition number and the thread rate in GB/s. The comment of line 38 says "best GB/s", but the code prints the rate of every repetition.
`fflush` writes the rows that the C library still holds in its buffer to the output.
Waits for the end of all benchmark threads. Then the process ends with exit status 0.
